description: Looking for talented devs who are interested in building a space game.
summary: Mythio is a browser-based 3D platform that turns any story brief into a playable world, and turns NASA's open data into something students can fly. Its Mission Control lab lets a learner assemble a mission — destination, launcher, bus, propulsion, power, communications, instruments, margins and budget — and watch mass, power, downlink and cost budgets update live. A deterministic engine grounded in NASA NSSDCA planetary fact sheets and NASA Glenn's rocket equation flies the simulation and returns an engineering debrief; the AI flight director only explains the stored record, never invents numbers. The same NASA textures and eight NASA 3D models become inspectable exhibits inside generated story missions, so learners meet Perseverance, Voyager, Bennu and the Deep Space Network as clues rather than captions. Every AI-written world is schema-validated and repaired before it ships, and a keyless generator keeps the whole platform usable without an API key or account. It answers the challenge by making NASA data playable: students learn engineering trade-offs by flying and failing missions, in six languages, on a normal browser, with every asset publicly credited.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mythio is a live, deployed web application (https://www.mythio.me) with two connected experiences.

Mission Control (`/mission-control`) is a mission-design laboratory. A student picks a destination, launch vehicle, spacecraft bus, propulsion, power source, antenna and instruments, then sets propellant margin, radiation shielding, redundancy and operations duration. Mass, power, downlink and cost budgets recalculate on every change, and blockers disable launch until the design is physically coherent. Launching runs a deterministic simulation — seeded, with no clock or random calls — that produces cruise ops, anomalies, science return, efficiency and a written debrief of design-specific lessons. The physics is real but simplified: propellant from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, solar generation scaled by NASA's published irradiance ratios, downlink falling with distance squared. Every assumed number (Δv budgets, derates, instrument specs, costs) is labelled a teaching assumption in the methodology, not a flight-certified value.

The story engine (`/create` → `/play`) compiles a plain-language brief into a walkable 3D world: locations, objects, clues, gated puzzles, missions and endings. Any AI provider can drive it (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, Groq, xAI, Mistral, NVIDIA NIM, Ollama, custom endpoints), or a deterministic keyless generator produces a complete tale with no account and no API key. Model output is never trusted: it passes through schema validation, a healing pass that resolves every objective onto a reachable target, and a playability gate, with one automatic retry that carries the validator's field report. Broken output never reaches a player. In Mars and space tales the compiler places a NASA Field Archive — eight real NASA models as inspectable exhibits feeding a clue-gated signal puzzle and a three-mission recovery arc.

NASA data and resources used

NASA NSSDCA planetary fact sheets (Earth, Moon, Mars, Venus, Jupiter) supply the irradiance values that drive the power budget and the gravity/radius/rotation reference facts. NASA Glenn's Ideal Rocket Equation and Specific Impulse pages define the propulsion model. NASA 3D Resources supplies five texture maps (Mars/Viking–USGS, Earth, Venus/Magellan, Jupiter/Voyager, plus NASA SVS's CGI Moon Kit from LRO/LROC and LOLA) and eight spacecraft GLBs: Perseverance, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Voyager, the 70-metre Deep Space Network dish, Bennu (1999 RQ36), James Webb, the Apollo Lunar Module and Hubble. An ESA/Hubble Jupiter observation (CC BY 4.0) illustrates the Jupiter destination. All are served locally, unmodified, with creator credits, source links and a SHA-256 asset manifest.

Benefits and intended impact

Space science is usually taught as facts to memorise. Mythio teaches it as decisions to make: adding an instrument costs mass, mass costs propellant, propellant costs margin, and a thin margin loses the mission. Students see the consequence immediately and try again. Because the engine is deterministic, a teacher can hand a whole class the same starting design and compare outcomes fairly. Because the story side is keyless and browser-only, a school with no budget, no API keys and no IT setup can still run it. NASA hardware stops being a photograph and becomes an object the learner walks up to, inspects and reasons about. The intended impact is a classroom-ready bridge between NASA's open data and people who would never open a fact sheet — game players, younger students, and non-English speakers (the interface ships in six languages).

Tools, languages and software

TypeScript end to end; React 19 with Three.js, React Three Fiber and drei for the 3D scene; Zustand for state; Zod for the world schema; a Fastify API with optional Neon Postgres cloud saves; Vite, esbuild and oxlint for the toolchain; Draco for mesh compression; Vitest and Playwright for testing; Vercel for hosting; GitHub for source control and asset provenance. Development ran in a Linux cloud developer environment on commodity hardware — no specialised equipment. Verification at submission: 299 unit tests across 44 files, three real-Chromium end-to-end suites (31 checks) covering mission design, NASA gameplay and the AI compile path, and a clean production build. A public credits ledger at https://www.mythio.me/credits lists every data source, all 339 locked packages with licences, fonts, services and development tools.

What makes it creative

Most space apps visualise data or quiz the learner. Mythio makes NASA data the *mechanic*. The same irradiance figure that sizes a solar array in Mission Control is a fact a player can discover in a story; the same Deep Space Network dish that closes a communication budget is the final activation in a puzzle chain. Coupling a grounded engineering simulator to a generative story engine — with a validator between the model and the player — is the novel part: the imagination is generated, the numbers are not.

Factors the team considered

Honesty first: the AI director explains stored simulation records and never recomputes engineering figures; assumptions are published; no live NASA feed or endorsement is implied. Licensing and attribution: NASA media guidelines followed, ESA/Hubble used under CC BY 4.0 with full credit, fonts under OFL, libraries under MIT/Apache, and a user-licensed local model importer that accepts only CC0/BY/BY-SA with mandatory creator metadata. Safety of generative output: schema validation, target healing and a playability gate before anything is filed. Privacy: user API keys stay in the browser and are never stored server-side. Access: keyless mode, six languages, no install, and a desktop-first 3D scene with a graceful handheld fallback.
